newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan alliance delays talks with U.N. envoy.
newsitem.headline: Afghan alliance delays talks with U.N. envoy.

text.p: An Afghan rebel alliance on Thursday postponed at the last minute talks with a United Nations peace envoy on a mission to head off a battle for the Afghan capital of Kabul.

U.N. officials in this northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif said the talks, scheduled for Thursday, were postponed until Friday because alliance leaders were out of Mazar-i-Sharif where the negotiations were to be held.
U.N. envoy Norbert Holl was informed of the postponement less than 12 hours before he was scheduled to fly to Mazar from Islamabad, the officials told Reuters.
"We have been told that General Abdul Malik and a delegate representing (Ahmed Shah) Masood cannot be in Mazar on Thursday," the officials said. "The talks have been rescheduled for Friday."
Malik and Masood, the ousted Afghan government's top military commander, are the main leaders of the alliance.

The last minute postponement added to speculation that a decisive battle was imminent between the alliance and Afghanistan's nominal government in Kabul, the Taleban, an Islamic fundamentalist grouping of mainly southern Afghan Pashtuns.

There were reports on Thursday in Mazar, the Afghan rebel headquarters, that the battle would not only be for Kabul but also for the western city of Herat, another Taleban stronghold that controls access to Iran, which supports the alliance.
Travellers just returned from the battle lines around Kabul reported that Masood had brought in nearly 1,000 more troops into his force and was ready for an attack on the capital at any moment.

Travellers just back from near Herat reported there were signs that Malik was massing troops in the area for a coordinated attack with Masood fighters on Herat, which the Taleban reinforced in recent days in anticipation of an attack.
"If the alliance captured Herat it would be almost as important strategically as Kabul, because the city controls key supply lines in Afghanistan," a U.N. source said.

With opposition forces poised less than 10 miles (16 km) from Kabul, within easy rocket and artillery range of the capital, Holl's mission was regarded as a final chance to avert a new cycle of violence that some analysts believe could lead to a de facto partition of Afghanistan into a northern and southern part.
The possible coming battle for Kabul puts the Taleban against a grouping of ethnic Uzbeks, Tajik and Hazaras who control the northern part of the country.

Holl's mission, described by U.N. sources in Mazar-i-Sharif as a fact finding tour, is to prepare for a visit in about one week's time of U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan's newly appointed special envoy for Afghanistan, Lakhdar Brahimi.
